title: Proof Before Permission: Vietnam Needs Dog-Trade Transparency
excerpt: Pet theft and rabies risk demand evidence, quarantine, and accountability. SDE calls for nationwide abolition by 2030—not unverified claims.
body_html:
A missing companion animal leaves a family facing loss; an unquarantined animal movement can leave communities facing exposure. Yet no police seizure, court conviction, location, date, or official trade record is documented here to prove claims about a specific dog-meat shipment or “dog farm.” That gap does not protect the trade. It demands transparent records, enforcement, and public scrutiny.

Myths cannot replace records

“Tradition” does not answer basic questions: Where did animals come from? Were they vaccinated? Were transport documents valid? Did veterinary authorities inspect and quarantine them? “Farm-raised” does not prove lawful origin. Operators must show traceable records. Without them, stolen pets, illegally moved animals, and lawful livestock cannot be treated as one category.

Biosecurity starts before exposure

Rabies risk belongs to bites, scratches, or infected saliva entering broken skin or mucous membranes—not to properly cooked meat as an established transmission route. After possible exposure, wash wounds with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seek urgent medical assessment. Post-exposure prophylaxis includes vaccination and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulin or approved monoclonal antibodies. Once symptoms appear, rabies is virtually 100% fatal. World Health Organization guidance supports rapid care.

Household exposure incidents and commercial transport chains are separate risks. Both show why quarantine, vaccination records, traceability, and enforcement matter. Vietnamese families, veterinarians, rescuers, and local reformers can demand those protections without shaming communities.

Demand an enforceable end

Regulation cannot excuse stolen companions or hidden supply chains. SDE calls for complete abolition by 2030. Sign the national petition. Add your name to a public demand for action, then follow campaign updates on how that demand reaches decision-makers.
